featured_items.title: 样例竞品异常讨论
featured_items.original_text:
USB-C. It’s a good cable sir. Just shitty signifiers that facilitate identification and communication. USB-C is obviously amazing, but I haven't really seen anyone discuss why so many protocols on a single connector are confusing to the user. They should have taken inspiration from industrial standards and required an extremely conspicuous signifier of two things: protocol (speed) and power delivery specs.

Ideally, the entire cable should be color-coded as they do in Fiber optics, telephone wiring, military, etc. The wire itself would indicate the power delivery capabilities and the connector housing color would signify the protocol it is capable of carrying. 

Currently, the USB standard has labeling requirements that are just terrible (logo) and only if it is certified. USB 3 if I remember correctly, added a blue tongue which was obvious in USB-A/B style connectors, but not so much with USB-C. You can’t easily search for it in a box of cables.

For example, connector colors:
Black = USB 2.0 (480 Mbps)
Blue = 5 Gbps (USB 3)
Red = 10 Gbps (USB 3)
Green = 20 Gbps (USB 3.2 2x2)
Orange = 40 Gbps (USB4 / TB3 / TB4)
Yellow = 80 Gbps (USB4 v2 / TB5)
White ring = active cable

Power delivery capacity:
Blue = 3A, 20V (60W)
Red = 5A, 20V (100W)
Yellow = 5A, 48V (240W)

The encoding scheme can be widened with striped colors on cables, rings on connectors, maybe dual colors. They already do this in several other standards like the 25-pair telephone wires with 5 ring colors and 5 tip colors. Or in Fiber optics: 12-fiber color sequence (blue, orange, green, brown, slate, white, red, black, yellow, violet, rose, aqua), with stripes for fibers 13–24. 

There is also association that forms over time: “Hey, find me a blue USB cable with an orange connector from that box.” People will start associating Green connector with USB 3.2 and so on. The lookup is precise: a blue wire with a yellow connector is precisely a 60W USB4 cable.

The USB consortium holds no authority besides just certification, so they can’t really force companies to follow the color coding guidelines and since it’s a consumer-slop temu industry, it inevitably gets flooded with garbage. We can't have nice things.
featured_items.translation_zh:
USB-C。先生，这是一根好线。只是那些用于帮助识别和沟通的标识太烂了。USB-C 显然很棒，但我还没怎么见过有人讨论为什么一个接口上有这么多协议会让用户困惑。他们本该从工业标准中汲取灵感，要求对两件事使用极其醒目的标识：协议（速度）和供电规格。

理想情况下，整根线缆都应该像光纤、电话布线、军用等领域那样进行颜色编码。线材本身表示供电能力，连接器外壳颜色则表示它能够承载的协议。

目前，USB 标准的标签要求非常糟糕（logo），而且只有在通过认证时才有。如果我没记错的话，USB 3 增加了一个蓝色舌片，这在 USB-A/B 这类接口上很明显，但在 USB-C 上就没那么明显。你没法在一盒线缆里轻松找到它。

例如，连接器颜色：
黑色 = USB 2.0（480 Mbps）
蓝色 = 5 Gbps（USB 3）
红色 = 10 Gbps（USB 3）
绿色 = 20 Gbps（USB 3.2 2x2）
橙色 = 40 Gbps（USB4 / TB3 / TB4）
黄色 = 80 Gbps（USB4 v2 / TB5）
白色环 = 主动式线缆

供电能力：
蓝色 = 3A，20V（60W）
红色 = 5A，20V（100W）
黄色 = 5A，48V（240W）

编码方案可以通过在线缆上使用条纹颜色、在连接器上使用色环，或许还有双色来扩展。他们已经在其他几个标准中这么做了，比如 25 对电话线使用 5 种环线颜色和 5 种尖线颜色。或者在光纤中：12 芯颜色序列（蓝色、橙色、绿色、棕色、石板灰、白色、红色、黑色、黄色、紫色、玫瑰色、水绿色），第 13–24 芯使用条纹。

还有一种会随着时间形成的关联：“嘿，从那个盒子里给我找一根蓝色 USB 线，带橙色连接器的。”人们会开始把绿色连接器和 USB 3.2 等联系起来。查找是精确的：一根蓝色线配黄色连接器，明确就是一根 60W USB4 线缆。

USB 联盟除了认证之外没有任何权力，所以他们实际上不能强迫公司遵循颜色编码指南；而且由于这是一个面向消费者的垃圾 Temu 式行业，它不可避免地会被垃圾产品淹没。我们就是没法拥有好东西。

top_posts.text:
USB-C. It’s a good cable sir. Just shitty signifiers that facilitate identification and communication. USB-C is obviously amazing, but I haven't really seen anyone discuss why so many protocols on a single connector are confusing to the user. They should have taken inspiration from industrial standards and required an extremely conspicuous signifier of two things: protocol (speed) and power delivery specs.

Ideally, the entire cable should be color-coded as they do in Fiber optics, telephone wiring, military, etc. The wire itself would indicate the power delivery capabilities and the connector housing color would signify the protocol it is capable of carrying. 

Currently, the USB standard has labeling requirements that are just terrible (logo) and only if it is certified. USB 3 if I remember correctly, added a blue tongue which was obvious in USB-A/B style connectors, but not so much with USB-C. You can’t easily search for it in a box of cables.

For example, connector colors:
Black = USB 2.0 (480 Mbps)
Blue = 5 Gbps (USB 3)
Red = 10 Gbps (USB 3)
Green = 20 Gbps (USB 3.2 2x2)
Orange = 40 Gbps (USB4 / TB3 / TB4)
Yellow = 80 Gbps (USB4 v2 / TB5)
White ring = active cable

Power delivery capacity:
Blue = 3A, 20V (60W)
Red = 5A, 20V (100W)
Yellow = 5A, 48V (240W)

The encoding scheme can be widened with striped colors on cables, rings on connectors, maybe dual colors. They already do this in several other standards like the 25-pair telephone wires with 5 ring colors and 5 tip colors. Or in Fiber optics: 12-fiber color sequence (blue, orange, green, brown, slate, white, red, black, yellow, violet, rose, aqua), with stripes for fibers 13–24. 

There is also association that forms over time: “Hey, find me a blue USB cable with an orange connector from that box.” People will start associating Green connector with USB 3.2 and so on. The lookup is precise: a blue wire with a yellow connector is precisely a 60W USB4 cable.

The USB consortium holds no authority besides just certification, so they can’t really force companies to follow the color coding guidelines and since it’s a consumer-slop temu industry, it inevitably gets flooded with garbage. We can't have nice things.
